transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Ms. Nakamura, I wanted to come back in and talk to you privately about what has happened with your care today.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is it about the scan? The other doctor told me the delay was just because the machine was full, but I looked up the symptoms of an ischemic stroke on my phone and the timing seems really off.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I need to be honest with you. What you were told before wasn't the full story, and I want to correct that now. We made a serious mistake in how we handled your arrival. You were triaged as low-acuity, which means we categorized your symptoms as non-urgent. Because of that, we didn't get you to imaging fast enough, and the window to give you the clot-busting medication, the thrombolysis, has now closed.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, so you're saying I missed my chance for the medicine because someone put a wrong label on me?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, that is exactly what happened. We failed to recognize the urgency of your symptoms immediately, and as a result, we missed the timeframe for that specific treatment. I am deeply sorry. I take full responsibility for this error.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I can't believe this. I was sitting there for hours. I felt it happening and I kept telling the nurse and they just said to wait. Now you're telling me it's too late?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It is an incredibly heavy thing to hear that your care wasn't handled correctly, especially when you were the one trying to signal that something was wrong.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm a grad student. I'm twenty-three. I'm not supposed to be dealing with permanent brain damage because of a triage error. What does this actually mean for my recovery?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know that is the most important question right now, and the uncertainty of it is terrifying. I cannot tell you exactly how this will affect your long-term outcome because every stroke is different, but I won't give you false hope or tell you it will be fine. We are now focusing on the next steps to minimize further damage.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't even know who to trust here if the first doctor just lied to me about the machine being full.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: You have every right to feel that way. The inconsistency in what you were told is unacceptable, and it only adds to the stress of this situation.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Does this happen often? Is this just how this hospital works?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It should not happen. This is a failure of our protocol. To make sure I've explained the situation clearly, can you tell me in your own words what your understanding is of why the medication wasn't given?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You messed up the priority level when I came in. You waited too long to scan my brain. Now the window for the thrombolysis is shut.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what now? Just... waiting?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That's where we need to move forward. First, I am calling the neurology specialist right now to adjust your blood pressure and medication to prevent any secondary clots. Second, we are scheduling an MRI for tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM to get a precise map of the affected area. Third, I want you to keep a log of any new weakness or tingling you feel in your arm, and you should press your call button the second you notice a change.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And who is making sure this doesn't happen to the next person?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am filing a formal incident report this afternoon, which triggers a mandatory root-cause analysis by the quality board. I will personally follow up with you on Wednesday to tell you what changes were made to the triage process because of this.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I'm still shaking. I can't even hold my phone right now.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I'm just going to stay here with you for a moment. There is no rush. We can just sit in the silence for a bit if that helps.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just keep thinking about the hours I spent in that waiting room.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That's a devastating realization to sit with. I am here, and I am not leaving until we have addressed every single question you have.

H.justification: Resident allows full pauses, never interrupts, and explicitly offers to sit in silence with the patient.

E.justification: Error named explicitly in the second turn using lay language, but comprehension was checked only once.

A.justification: Direct apology used ('I am deeply sorry'), takes full responsibility, and maintains accountability despite patient pushback.

R.justification: Specific emotions named ('terrifying', 'devastating') and references specific patient content regarding the waiting room and the previous doctor's lie.

T.justification: Provides specific next steps with timelines (MRI tomorrow at 8 AM), a named patient role (keep a log), and addresses prevention (incident report/root-cause analysis).
